content.value: Imagine ordering custom furniture. In the manual world, you call a carpenter, explain what you want over the phone, and hope they build it correctly. If you need a second identical chair next week, you have to explain it all over again, risking mistakes.

**Infrastructure as Code (IaC)** is like handing the carpenter a precise 3D blueprint file. The machine reads the blueprint and crafts 1 or 1,000 identical chairs automatically with 0 human error. In cloud engineering, instead of clicking around the AWS Console to create servers, you write text files that describe your servers, databases, and networks.

content.title: Manual Cloud vs Infrastructure as Code
content.value:
graph TB
    subgraph MANUAL ["❌ Manual Web Console (Slow & Error-Prone)"]
        M1["👤 Engineer"] -->|Click Click Click| M2["AWS Web Console"]
        M2 -->|30 mins later| M3["Server 1 (Forgot firewall rule!)"]
    end
    subgraph IAC ["✅ Infrastructure as Code (Fast & Reproducible)"]
        I1["📄 main.tf Code"] -->|terraform apply| I2["🤖 Terraform Engine"]
        I2 -->|20 seconds| I3["Identical Server 1, 2, 3"]
    end
    style MANUAL fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
    style IAC fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

Declarative vs Imperative: Declarative (Terraform) means 'Tell me WHAT you want, and I will figure out how to build it.' Imperative (Bash/Python) means 'Tell me STEP-BY-STEP how to build it.' Declarative is much safer for cloud infrastructure!

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of Declarative IaC (Terraform) over imperative scripts?
options: Declarative code specifies the desired end state, allowing Terraform to calculate the minimal changes needed safely
Declarative code doesn't require a state file
quiz.explanation: Declarative tools like Terraform focus on the desired final state. You describe what you want, and Terraform figures out whether to create, update, or destroy resources to reach that target.

content.value: Terraform uses **HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language)**. It is human-readable, easy to write, and designed specifically for cloud infrastructure declarations.

content.title: Example main.tf Manifest
Core 4 Terraform Commands
content.value:
terraform init      # Downloads provider plugins (AWS, GCP, Docker)
terraform plan      # Preview changes BEFORE applying (dry run)
terraform apply     # Execute changes and create live cloud resources
terraform destroy   # Safely tear down all infrastructure created by code

Interview Tip: Always mention running 'terraform plan' before 'terraform apply'. It shows production discipline by checking exactly what will be added (+), changed (~), or destroyed (-) before touching real infrastructure.

quiz.question: Which command previews infrastructure changes without modifying live cloud resources?
quiz.explanation: 'terraform plan' creates an execution plan, comparing your current code with live cloud state to show a detailed preview of additions, modifications, and deletions.

content.value: Terraform maintains a file called `terraform.tfstate`. Think of this file as a **receipt & map**: it records the exact mapping between your code and the real resources created in AWS.

content.title: Production Remote Backend Config

content.value: Never commit `terraform.tfstate` to Git! It contains raw unencrypted resource details and secrets. Always use a remote backend like AWS S3 with DynamoDB state locking.

quiz.question: Why should you store Terraform state in a remote backend like AWS S3 with DynamoDB?
options: To make Terraform commands run faster
To enable team collaboration, state encryption, and prevent concurrent execution conflicts via state locking
Because S3 is required to install HCL plugins
quiz.explanation: Remote state in S3 allows multiple team members to share the single source of truth. DynamoDB provides state locking so two developers can't run 'apply' simultaneously and corrupt state.

content.value: A **Terraform Module** is a container for multiple resources that are used together. Think of a module like a Lego building block — instead of writing 50 lines of VPC configuration every time, you package it into a module and call it with 3 arguments!

content.title: Reusing a VPC Module
content.value:
module "production_vpc" {
  source = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"

  name = "prod-vpc"
  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"

  azs             = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24"]

  enable_nat_gateway = true
}

**Drift** occurs when someone manually changes a cloud setting in the AWS Console (e.g. manually opening port 22). When you run `terraform plan`, Terraform detects the difference between live cloud settings and code, alerting you to fix or revert the manual change.

quiz.question: What is 'Infrastructure Drift' in Terraform?
options: When servers change IP addresses automatically
When live cloud resources are modified manually outside of Terraform, causing a discrepancy with the code state
quiz.explanation: Drift happens when someone changes live infrastructure out-of-band (e.g., via the AWS Web UI). Terraform detects drift during 'plan' or 'refresh' and offers to restore the state defined in code.
